ECE 6390 / Digital signals

Matched filter and timing

From the figure to the physics

Fig. 1 shows how an expected pulse shape becomes a receiver filter and a timing reference.

The receiver knows the shape it is trying to detect. For a finite discrete pulse s[n], a matched filter has impulse response h[n] = s*[N−1−n], where the star denotes complex conjugation. Time reversal and conjugation make a convolution output proportional to correlation with the expected pulse.

At the correct alignment, every desired pulse sample contributes with the same sign or phase. Independent white-noise samples add in variance, so this operation maximizes output SNR at the chosen sampling instant for a known waveform in white noise.

The peak location estimates timing. Noise, multipath and a wrong local waveform can move or split the peak. Matched filtering supplies a good decision statistic; acquisition and tracking still need to choose and maintain the correct alignment.

Example

The noiseless pulse [0.2, 0.5, 1, 0.5, 0.2] has aligned correlation 0.04 + 0.25 + 1 + 0.25 + 0.04 = 1.58. Its one-sample-shift overlap is smaller. Increasing the noise control lets you inspect whether the largest peak still marks the true arrival.

    Practice

    1. Why does the matched-filter definition reverse time and conjugate the pulse?

    Write a convolution and compare it with an inner product against a shifted template.

    Time reversal turns convolution into correlation. Conjugation cancels the expected complex phase, so aligned desired samples sum as |s[n]|².

    2. Would the matched filter for white noise remain optimal in strongly colored noise without modification?

    Frequency components no longer have equal noise strength.

    A colored-noise optimum generally weights the expected spectrum by inverse noise power, often described as whitening followed by matching. The simple reversed-conjugate pulse assumes white noise.
